summary: This memo discusses problems that arise, and debugging techniques used, when bringing a new network into operation. It is written in a light-hearted style.

plainLanguage.summary: Starting a new network is like turning on a brand-new machine, and things go wrong. This is a funny story about fixing them.

questions: how to debug a new network start-up
subtitle: A humorous guide to debugging new network startups.

tldr.problem: Bringing a new network into operation involves numerous interconnected systems and protocols that must all work together, and when they fail, the problems are difficult to diagnose.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 968 presents debugging techniques and problem-solving approaches in the form of a poem inspired by 'A Visit from St. Nicholas,' narrating how an experienced network engineer systematically troubleshoots a network startup that has failed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC conveys practical debugging wisdom through humor, showing how methodical examination of each component and protocol, combined with experience, can resolve even severe network failures.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: Poem (parody of 'A Visit from St. Nicholas')

today: RFC 968 is Informational and has become a classic in network engineering culture, fondly remembered for capturing the stress and humor of network debugging. While written in 1985, the RFC's core message about systematic troubleshooting and the frequency of simple errors remains relevant to network operators and engineers today.

sections.title: Network Startup Chaos
sections.content: RFC 968 discusses the problems and debugging techniques involved in bringing a new network into operation. The author captures the scene: it is the night before a scheduled network startup, no packets are moving, engineers are frustrated, and hope seems distant. The memo frames network debugging as a recognizable human drama with high stakes and complex systems, and offers the RFC as a way to share debugging experience and techniques with others who face similar challenges.
sections.plainLanguage: You switched on a new network, and nothing is working. Engineers are stressed. This RFC tells a funny story about fixing it.

sections.title: The Expert Debugger Arrives
sections.content: The poem introduces an experienced ARPANET hacker who arrives with methodology and confidence. This character methodically examines each alarm, the links (LAPB, OSI, X.25), and the protocols (TCP, SNA, V.35). The engineer works through the system with focused attention, checking each component for potential failure. The narrative shows how systematic inspection of each protocol layer and data link, combined with knowledge of how they should behave, reveals problems that seemed intractable to the initially frantic engineering team.
sections.plainLanguage: An expert shows up and calmly checks everything one piece at a time: the wires, the protocols, the hardware.

sections.title: The Debugging Lesson
sections.content: After careful troubleshooting, the expert identifies and fixes a critical problem. The network comes up: packets flow correctly, protocols match, hosts interface properly, and checksums are valid. Success appears imminent. However, the story ends with the author discovering that after all the debugging, a simple off-by-one indexing error in his own code was the cause. This final twist illustrates a common and humbling lesson in network debugging: the most obvious problems are often overlooked until everything else has been ruled out, and the cause is frequently simple, not complex.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything checks out perfect, but then you realize you made a silly mistake in counting something. That happens all the time.
